quests.sentence: She has finished the presentation.
quests.ruleExplanation: Has finished pairs the present-tense helper has with the past participle to connect a completed action to the present, followed by the object the report.
quests.nativeTip: Have/has plus the past participle links a past action to now, followed by the object.

quests.sentence: They have completed the project.
quests.ruleExplanation: Have completed pairs the plural subject They with the past participle, followed by the object the project.
quests.nativeTip: A plural subject takes have, still followed directly by the past participle and object.

quests.sentence: I have submitted my application.
quests.ruleExplanation: Have submitted is the correct pairing for I, followed by the object my application.
quests.nativeTip: I always takes have, never has, before the past participle.

quests.sentence: He has already left the office.
quests.ruleExplanation: Already sits between has and left, right in the middle of the present perfect verb phrase, before the past participle.
quests.nativeTip: Already slots in between has/have and the past participle, emphasizing something happened sooner than expected.

quests.sentence: They have already signed the contract.
quests.ruleExplanation: Already comes between have and signed, keeping its position right before the past participle regardless of subject.
quests.nativeTip: The same mid-position applies with a plural subject: have, then already, then the past participle.

quests.sentence: She has already reviewed the proposal.
quests.ruleExplanation: Already fits between has and reviewed, following the same fixed position seen in the previous two sentences.
quests.nativeTip: Already always sits in that same spot, between the helper verb and the past participle.

quests.sentence: I have just finished my lunch.
quests.ruleExplanation: Just sits between have and finished, indicating the action happened only moments before now.
quests.nativeTip: Just occupies the same mid-position as already, showing something happened a very short time ago.

quests.sentence: She has just returned from vacation.
quests.ruleExplanation: Just comes between has and returned, with from vacation completing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The same mid-position rule applies: has, then just, then the past participle.

quests.sentence: They have just released the update.
quests.ruleExplanation: Just fits between have and released, followed by the object the update.
quests.nativeTip: Just still sits in that middle slot, right before the past participle.

quests.sentence: Have you finished the report yet?
quests.ruleExplanation: Have inverts to the front to form the question, and yet closes the sentence after the object the report, asking if something happened up to now.
quests.nativeTip: Yet goes at the very end of a present perfect question, after the object.

quests.sentence: Has she called the client yet?
quests.ruleExplanation: Has opens the question before she, and yet closes it after the object the client.
quests.nativeTip: The same end-position rule for yet applies with has, for a singular subject.

quests.sentence: Have they announced the results yet?
quests.ruleExplanation: Have leads the question before they, and yet closes it after the object the results.
quests.nativeTip: Yet still closes the question, no matter which subject or object appears.

quests.sentence: She hasn't finished the proposal yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: Hasn't replaces has not before finished, and yet closes the sentence, matching the question pattern but in negative form.
quests.nativeTip: Hasn't fuses has and not, and yet still closes the sentence at the end.

quests.sentence: We haven't received the payment yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: Haven't stands in for have not before received, and yet closes the sentence after the payment.
quests.nativeTip: Haven't works the same way for a plural subject, with yet still at the end.

quests.sentence: They haven't announced a decision yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: Haven't precedes announced, and yet closes the sentence after a decision, following the established negative-plus-yet pattern.
quests.nativeTip: The negative contraction still comes before the past participle, with yet closing things off.

quests.sentence: Have you ever visited Japan?
quests.ruleExplanation: Have inverts to the front, and ever follows it directly before visited, asking about experience at any point in life.
quests.nativeTip: Ever sits right after the inverted have/has, asking about any time up to now.

quests.sentence: Has she ever missed a deadline?
quests.ruleExplanation: Has opens the question, she follows, and ever comes right before missed, in the same slot as the previous sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The same position for ever applies with has, right after the subject.

quests.sentence: Have they ever canceled an order?
quests.ruleExplanation: Have leads the question, they follows, and ever precedes canceled, with an order as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Ever keeps its position right before the past participle, regardless of subject or object.

quests.sentence: I have never tried sushi.
quests.ruleExplanation: Never combines the meaning of not and ever into one word, sitting between have and tried without needing an extra not.
quests.nativeTip: Never already means 'not ever', so no separate 'not' is needed — it sits in the same mid-position.

quests.sentence: She has never missed a meeting.
quests.ruleExplanation: Never fits between has and missed, expressing a negative meaning without any separate not.
quests.nativeTip: The same mid-position rule applies: has, then never, then the past participle.

quests.sentence: They have never visited this country.
quests.ruleExplanation: Never comes between have and visited, with this country as the object, keeping the built-in negative meaning.
quests.nativeTip: Never still sits in that same slot, right before the past participle.

quests.sentence: He has worked here since March.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since March names the specific point when the action began, closing the sentence after has worked here.
quests.nativeTip: Since names a starting point in time and closes the sentence, right after the verb phrase.

quests.sentence: She has lived in Chicago since 2015.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 2015 names the starting point of an ongoing situation, following in Chicago and closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Since works the same way with a specific year, marking exactly when the situation started.

quests.sentence: They have used this software since last year.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since last year marks when the use of this software began, closing the sentence after the object this software.
quests.nativeTip: Since can also pair with a phrase like last year to mark a starting point.

quests.sentence: He has worked here for five years.
quests.ruleExplanation: For five years states the duration of the action, closing the sentence after has worked here — contrast this with since, which marks a starting point instead.
quests.nativeTip: For introduces a length of time rather than a starting point, and it closes the sentence.

quests.sentence: She has studied English for two months.
quests.ruleExplanation: For two months states how long she has studied English, closing the sentence with a duration rather than a starting point.
quests.nativeTip: The same duration pattern applies here: for plus a length of time at the end.

quests.sentence: They have known each other for a decade.
quests.ruleExplanation: For a decade closes the sentence, stating the duration of knowing each other, which comes right after the verb known.
quests.nativeTip: For still introduces the duration, even with a longer object phrase before it.

quests.sentence: She has already worked here for three years.
quests.ruleExplanation: Already sits between has and worked, and for three years (duration) closes the sentence, combining two skills from this file.
quests.nativeTip: Combine already in its usual mid-position with a for-duration phrase at the end.

quests.sentence: He hasn't traveled abroad since last summer.
quests.ruleExplanation: Hasn't precedes traveled, and since last summer (a starting point) closes the sentence, pairing the negative form with since.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a negative contraction with a since-point-in-time phrase at the end.

quests.sentence: Have they already reviewed the new proposal?
quests.ruleExplanation: Have opens the question before they, and already sits before reviewed, combining the question inversion with the already pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Combine the question pattern with already in its familiar mid-position.
